title: Hide Artifacts: Email Hiding Rules
summary: Email Hiding Rules abuse the rule engine inside a mailbox or a mail transport to divert messages the adversary does not want read. Rules can move mail into low visibility folders, mark it as read, forward it elsewhere or delete it, and they commonly filter on ordinary message content such as keywords, senders or subjects. They can be created from a mail client or remotely through mailbox management cmdlets and interfaces. Mailbox audit records capture rule creation and modification, folder moves and deletions, so a defender can pair an unusual rule with the messages that subsequently disappeared. Separating malicious rules from user sorting depends on who made the change, when, and whether the rule targets security vocabulary.

beginner.definition: Email programs let you create rules to sort your mail. A rule can move a message into a folder, mark it as read, or delete it. Attackers create rules that quietly hide warning emails. The messages still arrive, but the user never sees them.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security alerts often arrive by email. If a rule hides those messages, the user and the defenders stay blind. The attacker gains time to keep working inside the account. Other staff may reply to emails the attacker sent, and those replies are hidden as well. A single mailbox rule can therefore hide a whole conversation from the people who need it.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to a mailbox, using stolen passwords or a hijacked session.
They create a rule that looks for words such as alert, suspicious or invoice in incoming mail.
The rule then moves matching messages into a folder the user rarely opens.
Some rules also mark messages as read, so a quick glance shows nothing unread.
Other rules forward copies to an outside address, or delete the message straight away.
Large organisations can also run transport rules that act on all mail before delivery.
beginner.example: Imagine the post room of a large office. Every morning a clerk sorts the letters into pigeonholes for each department. Someone slips the clerk a new instruction. From now on, all letters marked urgent must go into a storage cupboard instead of a pigeonhole. The letters still arrive, and the post room log still shows them. But the departments never see the warnings, and they carry on as if nothing happened. An email hiding rule is that new instruction to the clerk.
takeaways: Mailbox rules can hide security warnings without deleting anything visible.
Review rule creation events and the folders that messages were moved into.
Unexpected rules that match words such as alert or phish are a red flag.

objectives: Explain how mail rules work in a normal mailbox.
Describe how an attacker uses rules to hide or redirect messages.
List the audit records that show rule creation and message movement.
Compare ordinary user sorting rules with malicious hiding rules.
Outline the response steps to take when a malicious rule is discovered.
